repository.title: Battery and Power Reference Lab
repository.description: Explore battery thermal balances & DC-link sizing through inspectable Python and MATLAB models with reproducible checks.
repository.summary: Dependency-free Python references and MATLAB equivalents cover lumped battery heating and DC-link sizing. The browser lab follows the thermal balance and directs electrical sizing questions to the native functions.
repository.audience: Engineers and students making early thermal and power-electronics sensitivity checks.

model.equation: ΔT = (Q/h) · (1 − exp(−h · 60t/C)); T = Tₐ + ΔT; heat removed = hΔT; stored heat = CΔT/1000.
assumptions: One uniform thermal mass starts at ambient temperature.
Constant heat input and linear heat transfer; no phase change or spatial gradients.
Elapsed time is shown in minutes; the energy-balance calculation uses seconds.
Browser heat, conductance, and thermal capacity are illustrative teaching inputs, not the native default cell parameters.
One thermal mass cannot predict internal gradients or qualify a battery cooling design.
DC-link ripple and energy-pulse capacitance are separate native calculations and are not derived from this temperature graph.
model.introduction: The browser uses the same first-order energy-balance form with a different, explicitly illustrative scale. It takes heat directly in watts; the native thermal model derives heat from current squared times resistance.

modules.title: Balance generated and rejected heat
modules.objective: Use steady-state rise and the time constant to predict a first-order response.
steps: Read ThermalParameters and analytical_step in src/battery_thermal.py.
Apply 300 W heat, 20 W/K cooling, 6,000 J/K thermal capacity, and 25°C ambient.
Predict the asymptotic rise of 15 K and the five-minute time constant, then run.
modules.reflection: Why does the same temperature difference have the same numerical value in kelvin and degrees Celsius?

modules.title: Translate a current change into heat
modules.objective: Recognize quadratic Joule heating while holding the thermal path fixed.
steps: Treat the baseline 300 W as I²R for an illustrative operating point.
Double current conceptually while keeping resistance fixed; set heat to 1,200 W.
Predict a fourfold steady temperature rise and compare the one-hour result.
modules.reflection: Why would a real cell with temperature-dependent resistance deviate from this constant-parameter comparison?

modules.title: Choose a cooling sensitivity
modules.objective: Separate the effects of cooling conductance on steady rise and response time.
steps: Keep heat at 1,200 W and thermal capacity at 6,000 J/K.
Increase conductance from 20 to 80 W/K and predict both response speed and final temperature.
Read the test that compares weak and strong cooling in the native model.
modules.reflection: Why is specifying a conductance different from selecting a fan, cold plate, or coolant flow rate?

modules.title: Transfer the accounting habit to DC-link sizing
modules.objective: Keep energy, power, waveform, and boundary assumptions explicit across two reference models.
steps: Use 1,200 W, 80 W/K, 60,000 J/K, and 35°C ambient to inspect a slower thermal transient.
At ten minutes, reconcile stored heat with temperature rise and thermal capacity.
Read the two functions in src/dc_link.py and identify which uses a triangular current waveform and which uses capacitor-energy change.
modules.reflection: What additional component tolerances, switching behavior, or control dynamics would be needed before selecting a DC-link capacitor?
